note: Substantive lessons written after the first pass: constitutional structure, the general exceptions, criminal procedure, contract remedies, tort, land, company, evidence, civil procedure and administrative law. Ordered after the lessons in substantive.json within each module.

lessons.title: The federal bargain: who may legislate on what
lessons.summary: The Ninth Schedule divides legislative power into three lists. Article 75 decides what happens when federal and state law collide, and most constitutional problems begin here.

body.text: Malaysia is a federation. Parliament legislates for the Federation; each State Legislative Assembly legislates for its State. Neither has general power: each may only legislate on the subjects allotted to it, and a law outside the allotted field is invalid however sensible it is.
Parliament may make laws with respect to matters in the Federal List and the Concurrent List; a State Legislature may make laws with respect to matters in the State List and the Concurrent List.
body.source: Federal Constitution Arts 74(1) and 74(2), read with the Ninth Schedule

body.text: The Ninth Schedule contains three lists: List I (Federal), List II (State) and List III (Concurrent). There are also supplementary lists for Sabah and Sarawak, which is one of several ways in which the two Bornean States sit differently in the federation.

sections.h: What is in which list, in outline

items: **Federal List** — external affairs, defence, internal security, civil and criminal law and procedure, the administration of justice, citizenship, finance, trade and commerce, communications, education, medicine and health.

**State List** — Islamic law and personal and family law of persons professing the religion of Islam, Malay custom, land, agriculture and forestry, local government, State works and water, State holidays.
**Concurrent List** — social welfare, scholarships, protection of wild animals and wild birds, town and country planning, drainage and irrigation, public health, and others.

body.text: Notice what is federal and counter-intuitive: **land** is a State matter, but the National Land Code is a federal statute. That is possible because of Art 76, which lets Parliament legislate on State matters for the purpose of uniformity, with the law taking effect in a State only when adopted by its legislature. If you cannot explain that, you will misstate the Torrens material later.
If any State law is inconsistent with a federal law, the federal law shall prevail and the State law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.

Two things follow. First, the State law is not wholly void — only to the extent of the inconsistency, and severance is the ordinary course. Second, the question is prior: before Art 75 can operate at all, the federal law must itself be within federal competence. A federal statute outside List I and List III does not prevail over anything; it is invalid under Art 4(1).

A State enactment regulating the licensing of a trade collides with a federal statute doing the same. The first question is not which prevails — it is whether trade and commerce is a federal subject at all. Only if the federal law is valid does Art 75 do any work.

sections.h: Article 4(1), and how invalidity is raised

body.text: This Constitution is the supreme law of the Federation and any law passed after Merdeka Day which is inconsistent with this Constitution shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void.

Supremacy is the whole of the reason a legislative-competence argument is available. In a system of parliamentary sovereignty the question does not arise; here it is the first question about any statute.

Art 4(3) and 4(4) restrict how a challenge to the *validity of a law on the ground of legislative competence* may be brought, including a leave requirement for proceedings in the Federal Court. Check the current text and the current practice before asserting how such a challenge must be commenced — this is a procedural trap rather than a substantive one, and it is where competent answers lose marks.

sections.h: Why this is the first constitutional lesson and not the fourth

body.text: A fundamental liberties problem usually turns on whether a restriction is authorised. But a restriction imposed by a law the legislature had no power to pass fails before Article 10 is reached, and an answer that goes straight to proportionality has skipped a complete and often decisive argument.
The discipline is: competence first, then constitutionality of content, then the ordinary construction of the provision.

quiz.q: Under which Article does federal law prevail over inconsistent State law?
quiz.why: Art 75 is the inconsistency provision; the State law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.

quiz.q: Land is a State matter, yet the National Land Code is a federal statute. What makes that possible?
options: Art 76, which permits Parliament to legislate on State matters for uniformity
Land is in fact on the Federal List
quiz.why: Art 76 is the uniformity route, and the law takes effect in a State on adoption by its legislature.

quiz.q: A federal statute is passed on a subject in the State List. What is the position?
options: It is invalid; Art 75 never arises
It is valid if the State consents afterwards
quiz.why: Art 75 presupposes a valid federal law. Competence is the prior question, under Art 4(1).

quiz.q: Which of these is a State matter?
quiz.why: List II includes Islamic law, personal and family law of Muslims, Malay custom, land and local government.

quiz.q: What does Art 4(1) provide?
options: The Constitution is supreme and inconsistent law is void to that extent
Federal law prevails over State law
The courts may not review legislation
quiz.why: Supremacy is what makes a competence argument available at all.

quiz.q: In a fundamental liberties problem, what should be checked before proportionality?
options: Whether the legislature had power to pass the law at all
quiz.why: A restriction in an ultra vires statute fails without ever reaching Art 10.

lessons.source: Federal Constitution Arts 4(1), 74, 75, 76 and the Ninth Schedule (Lists I, II and III).
lessons.verify: Check the current text of the Ninth Schedule — items have been moved and added over time — and check Arts 4(3) and 4(4) and the current Federal Court practice on how a legislative-competence challenge must be brought.

lessons.title: Judicial power, Article 121, and the argument about basic structure
lessons.summary: The 1988 amendment to Article 121(1) removed the words vesting judicial power in the courts. What survived that amendment is one of the live questions in Malaysian constitutional law.

sections.h: What Article 121(1) said, and what it says

body.text: Before 1988, Art 121(1) provided that the judicial power of the Federation shall be vested in two High Courts and in such inferior courts as may be provided by federal law. The 1988 amendment replaced that formula: the High Courts and inferior courts now 'shall have such jurisdiction and powers as may be conferred by or under federal law'.

On one reading that made the courts' jurisdiction entirely a creature of statute. On another, judicial power is inherent in a constitution that separates the branches, and cannot be removed by amending the sentence that describes it. Both readings have been taken by Malaysian courts.
This is a moving area and a favourite examination topic precisely because it is unsettled. Do not state either position as settled law without checking the most recent Federal Court authority.
The courts referred to in Clause (1) shall have no jurisdiction in respect of any matter within the jurisdiction of the Syariah courts.

Clause (1A) is not a grant of power to the Syariah courts. It is a removal of jurisdiction from the civil courts over matters already within Syariah jurisdiction, and the Syariah courts' own jurisdiction comes from State enactments under List II. The distinction matters: if the matter is outside Syariah jurisdiction, (1A) does nothing and the civil court retains its power.

The hardest cases are those where a single dispute has both civil and Syariah aspects — the status of a person, the custody of a child, the disposal of a body — and the answer usually turns on how the question is characterised rather than on any disagreement about the rule.

The argument is that certain features of the Constitution — judicial power, the rule of law, the separation of powers — are so fundamental that Parliament cannot remove them even by a validly passed constitutional amendment. Its origin is Indian, and it has been received in Malaysia unevenly.

The Malaysian position has changed direction more than once. There are Federal Court decisions rejecting the doctrine and later ones applying it. If you write about this, write about the sequence and its current state, and give the citations — an assertion with no case name is worth nothing here.

The practical use of the doctrine is narrow. It is an argument of last resort against an amendment, not a general licence to strike down legislation, and confusing the two is the commonest error in an answer on it.

sections.h: Article 128 and where a constitutional question goes

items: The Federal Court has exclusive jurisdiction to determine whether a law made by Parliament or a State Legislature is invalid on the ground that it relates to a matter outside legislative competence.
It also determines disputes between States, or between the Federation and a State.
A constitutional question arising in proceedings in the High Court may be referred to the Federal Court; the mechanism and its limits are in the Constitution and the Courts of Judicature Act 1964.

body.text: Getting the forum right is a method point, and method is a rubric band. An answer that reaches the correct constitutional conclusion in the wrong court has not advised the client.

quiz.q: What did the 1988 amendment do to Art 121(1)?
options: Replaced the vesting of judicial power with jurisdiction conferred by federal law
quiz.why: The vesting formula was replaced by a conferral formula, and the consequences of that are still argued.

quiz.q: What does Art 121(1A) do?
options: Removes civil court jurisdiction over matters within Syariah jurisdiction
Grants jurisdiction to the Syariah courts
Creates a right of appeal to the Federal Court
quiz.why: It is a subtraction from the civil courts, not a grant. Syariah jurisdiction itself comes from State enactments.

quiz.q: If a matter falls outside Syariah jurisdiction, what follows for Art 121(1A)?
options: It does not apply and the civil court retains jurisdiction
The civil court still has no jurisdiction
quiz.why: (1A) only bites where the matter is within Syariah jurisdiction in the first place.

quiz.q: What is the basic structure doctrine, at its narrowest?
options: That certain fundamental features cannot be removed even by constitutional amendment
That all legislation must be proportionate
That the Federal Court may overrule itself
That State law yields to federal law
quiz.why: It is a limit on the amending power, not a general power of review.

quiz.q: Which court determines whether a law is invalid for want of legislative competence?
options: Any court seised of the matter
quiz.why: Article 128 gives the Federal Court exclusive jurisdiction on that question.

reading.where: the treatment of judicial power and the 1988 amendments

lessons.source: Federal Constitution Arts 121(1), 121(1A) and 128; the Constitution (Amendment) Act 1988; the Malaysian case law on judicial power and basic structure.
lessons.verify: This is the most unsettled area in this module. Before relying on anything above, find the most recent Federal Court decision on judicial power and on basic structure and read it in full — the direction of authority has reversed before and the case names matter more than the summary.

lessons.title: General exceptions, and who has to prove what
lessons.summary: Chapter IV of the Penal Code applies to every offence in it. The burden of bringing yourself within an exception is on the accused, and it is a burden on the balance of probabilities.

body.text: The general exceptions in sections 76 to 106 of the Penal Code are not defences to particular offences. They apply to every offence in the Code, and to offences under other statutes so far as the Code's general provisions are made applicable.

Every definition of an offence in the Penal Code is to be understood subject to the exceptions in the Chapter entitled 'General Exceptions', though those exceptions are not repeated in the definition itself.
That is why a homicide answer that discusses the exceptions to s 300 without ever asking about private defence or unsoundness of mind has looked at only half the picture.

items: **Mistake and justification** — ss 76 and 79: an act done by a person bound, or who by mistake of fact in good faith believes himself bound or justified by law, to do it. Mistake of *fact*, not of law.
**Judicial and official acts** — ss 77 and 78.
**Accident** — s 80: an accident or misfortune, without criminal intention or knowledge, in the doing of a lawful act by lawful means with proper care and caution.
**Necessity** — s 81: an act likely to cause harm done without criminal intention and in good faith to prevent other harm to person or property.
**Infancy** — ss 82 and 83: nothing is an offence done by a child under ten; and by a child of ten and under twelve who has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding.
**Unsoundness of mind** — s 84: a person incapable, by reason of unsoundness of mind, of knowing the nature of the act, or that it is wrong or contrary to law.
**Intoxication** — ss 85 and 86, which are narrow: involuntary intoxication, or intoxication producing insanity.
**Consent** — ss 87 to 92, with limits by age and by degree of harm.
**Private defence** — ss 96 to 106, of the body and of property.

sections.h: Private defence is where the marks are

body.text: Private defence is the exception that appears most often in problem questions because it is a matter of degree and therefore genuinely arguable. Two things structure it.

There is no right of private defence against an act which does not reasonably cause the apprehension of death or grievous hurt, if there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities; and the right in no case extends to inflicting more harm than is necessary.

Section 100 sets out the cases in which the right of private defence of the body extends to causing death — reasonable apprehension of death, of grievous hurt, and certain enumerated offences. Section 103 does the same for property.

The commonest error is to treat the right as lost because the response was excessive. Excess goes to whether the right extended *this far*, and an accused who exceeds the right may still reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Exception 2 to s 300. Losing that point is losing the difference between a mandatory and a discretionary sentence.

When a person is accused of any offence, the burden of proving the existence of circumstances bringing the case within any of the General Exceptions in the Penal Code is upon him, and the court shall presume the absence of those circumstances.

That is a legal burden on the accused, and it is discharged on the balance of probabilities — not beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution's burden of proving the offence itself is unaffected and remains throughout.

Do not write that the accused must 'raise' the exception and the prosecution must then disprove it beyond reasonable doubt. That is the English position on some defences and it is not what s 105 says.

quiz.q: Where does the burden of proving a general exception lie?
options: On the accused, on the balance of probabilities
On the prosecution, beyond reasonable doubt
On the accused, beyond reasonable doubt
It is a purely evidential burden
quiz.why: Section 105 of the Evidence Act places a legal burden on the accused and directs the court to presume the absence of the circumstances.

quiz.q: Section 79 of the Penal Code excuses an act done under a mistake of what?
quiz.why: Mistake of fact in good faith, believing oneself justified by law. Mistake of law does not excuse.

quiz.q: Under s 82, a child under what age cannot commit an offence at all?
quiz.why: Nothing is an offence which is done by a child under ten; between ten and twelve, sufficient maturity of understanding is the question.

quiz.q: An accused exceeds the right of private defence and kills. What is the most likely effect?
options: Murder may be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder
The right is simply lost and murder stands
It is a complete defence anyway
quiz.why: Exception 2 to s 300 addresses exceeding the right of private defence in good faith and without premeditation.

quiz.q: Under s 99(3), when is there no right of private defence?
options: Where there is time to have recourse to the public authorities and no apprehension of death or grievous hurt
Whenever the police could be called
quiz.why: The provision is conditional on the absence of reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.

quiz.q: Why does Chapter IV matter to a homicide answer?
options: The exceptions apply to every offence in the Code, including s 300
They apply only to offences against property
They replace the exceptions to s 300
They apply only in the Sessions Court
quiz.why: Section 6 makes every definition subject to the general exceptions.

lessons.source: Penal Code ss 6, 76-106, and Exception 2 to s 300; Evidence Act 1950 s 105.

lessons.title: Bail, and the shape of a criminal trial
lessons.summary: Whether bail is available turns on how the offence is classified. The trial then has two decision points — the close of the prosecution case and the close of the defence — and they ask different questions.

body.text: The classification is done by the First Schedule to the Criminal Procedure Code, offence by offence. The vocabulary misleads: 'non-bailable' does not mean bail is unavailable.

items: **Bailable offence** — the accused is entitled to be released on bail. It is not a discretion.
**Non-bailable offence** — bail is in the discretion of the court, subject to the restrictions in s 388.

**Offences punishable with death or imprisonment for life** — the general position under s 388(1) is that a person shall not be released on bail, subject to the provisos in the section, which include provision for young persons, women, and the sick or infirm.

body.text: A person accused of a bailable offence shall be released on bail; a person accused of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail, in the discretion of the court.
Some statutes outside the Code create their own bail regimes, and some exclude bail altogether. Always check the statute creating the offence before applying the Code's scheme.

sections.h: What the discretion is exercised on

body.text: Where bail is discretionary the court asks whether the accused will attend trial, and whether release presents risks the conditions cannot manage: interference with witnesses, the gravity of the offence and the likely sentence, the accused's antecedents and ties, the state of the investigation.
Conditions — sureties, surrender of a passport, reporting — are how those risks are managed, and a proposal of conditions is usually a better answer than an assertion that the risk is low.

A person arrested shall be informed as soon as may be of the grounds of his arrest and shall be allowed to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice; and shall not be detained beyond twenty-four hours without the authority of a Magistrate.
body.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(3) and 5(4), reflected in the Criminal Procedure Code

body.text: Detention beyond twenty-four hours requires a remand order from a Magistrate under s 117 of the Code, for the purpose of investigation, for the period the Magistrate thinks fit within the statutory maximum. The remand hearing is a real hearing, not a formality, and the police must show why further detention is needed.
Check the current maximum remand periods in s 117 — they are graduated by the length of the sentence the offence carries and have been amended.

sections.h: The two decision points at trial

body.text: At the close of the case for the prosecution the court shall consider whether the prosecution has made out a prima facie case; if it has, the court shall call upon the accused to enter his defence, and if it has not, the court shall record an order of acquittal.

A prima facie case is made out where the evidence, if unrebutted, would warrant a conviction. That standard has been the subject of amendment and of a good deal of judicial discussion — the phrase 'maximum evaluation' comes from that discussion, and it means the court must evaluate the prosecution evidence properly at this stage rather than merely ask whether some evidence exists.

At the close of the defence the question is different and simple: has the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt on the whole of the evidence? A defence that raises a reasonable doubt is enough; it does not have to be believed.

Do not merge the two. Writing that the accused must 'prove' his defence at the second stage is wrong except where a statute places a burden on him — as s 105 of the Evidence Act does for the general exceptions.

sections.h: Who prosecutes, and who may withdraw

body.text: The Public Prosecutor has control and direction of all criminal prosecutions under Art 145(3) of the Federal Constitution. A discharge not amounting to an acquittal leaves the prosecution able to recharge; an acquittal does not. The difference is worth stating precisely, because clients hear 'discharged' and understand 'finished'.

quiz.q: What does 'non-bailable offence' mean?
options: Bail is in the court's discretion
Bail requires the Public Prosecutor's consent
Bail is granted only on appeal
quiz.why: The label is misleading. Section 388 makes bail discretionary for these offences, subject to its restrictions.

quiz.q: Where is an offence classified as bailable or non-bailable?
options: The First Schedule to the Criminal Procedure Code
quiz.why: Classification is done offence by offence in the First Schedule.

quiz.q: How long may a person be detained after arrest without a Magistrate's authority?
quiz.why: Art 5(4) sets twenty-four hours; further detention needs a remand order under s 117 CPC.

quiz.q: What is the question at the close of the prosecution case?
options: Whether a prima facie case has been made out
Whether guilt is proved beyond reasonable doubt
Whether the accused has a defence
Whether the charge is properly framed
quiz.why: Section 180. If a prima facie case is made out the accused is called on to enter his defence.

quiz.q: At the close of the defence, what must the accused's evidence achieve?
options: Prove innocence on the balance of probabilities
quiz.why: The prosecution's burden never shifts, save where a statute places one on the accused.

quiz.q: What is the effect of a discharge not amounting to an acquittal?
options: The accused may be recharged on the same facts
The prosecution is at an end
It is the same as an acquittal
quiz.why: It is not a final determination, which is precisely why the distinction has to be explained to a client.

lessons.title: Vitiating factors: when an agreement can be undone
lessons.summary: Free consent is defined by what removes it. Coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation and mistake are each defined by section, and each has a different consequence.

sections.h: Start from the definition, not from the English cases

body.text: An agreement is a contract if it is made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and is not expressly declared to be void.
Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake.

Section 14 is a closed list with statutory definitions in the sections that follow. An answer that reasons from English duress or English misrepresentation without going through ss 15 to 23 has started in the wrong place, and it usually gets the consequence wrong as well.

items: **Coercion (s 15)** — committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the Penal Code, or unlawfully detaining or threatening to detain any property, to the prejudice of any person, with the intention of causing a person to enter into an agreement. Note how much narrower the statutory definition is than 'pressure'.

**Undue influence (s 16)** — where the relations between the parties are such that one is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage. Section 16(2) gives instances; s 16(3) shifts the burden to the dominant party where the transaction appears unconscionable.

**Fraud (s 17)** — the suggestion of a fact that is untrue by one who does not believe it to be true; active concealment; a promise made without intention of performing it; and other acts fitted to deceive. Mere silence is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak, or silence is in itself equivalent to speech.

**Misrepresentation (s 18)** — a positive assertion, not warranted by the information of the person making it, of that which is not true though he believes it to be true; certain breaches of duty; and causing a party to make a mistake as to the subject-matter. Innocent, in other words, in a way s 17 is not.
**Mistake (ss 21-23)** — a mistake of both parties as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement makes it void; a mistake as to a law in force in Malaysia does not.

sections.h: The consequence is not the same for all of them

body.text: When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.

Voidable means valid until avoided, at the election of the innocent party, and the right to rescind can be lost — by affirmation, by lapse of time, or where restitution has become impossible. Bilateral mistake as to an essential fact, by contrast, makes the agreement **void** under s 21: there is nothing to affirm.

Section 66 then deals with restoration: a person who has received an advantage under an agreement discovered to be void, or a contract that becomes void, must restore it or make compensation. It is the provision that does the work an English lawyer would look for in restitution.

Section 11 makes a person competent to contract if of the age of majority, of sound mind, and not disqualified from contracting by law. The age of majority is eighteen under the Age of Majority Act 1971, and the consequences of a minor's agreement in Malaysia are governed by the Act and the local authorities rather than by the English infancy rules.

The consideration or object of an agreement is unlawful if it is forbidden by law, or would defeat any law, or is fraudulent, or involves injury to person or property, or the court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy; every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful is void.
Do not reach for 'illegality' as a general doctrine. Section 24 lists the categories and s 25 deals with partial illegality; the argument in a real case is about which paragraph of s 24 is engaged.

Name the vitiating factor and its section. State the statutory definition. Apply it to the facts, both ways where it is arguable. Then state the consequence — void or voidable — and what follows from that for the remedy sought. Answers lose marks in the last step far more often than the first.

quiz.q: Under the Contracts Act 1950, what is the effect of a bilateral mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement?
options: The agreement is unenforceable but not void
quiz.why: Section 21 makes it void. Voidability under s 19 applies to coercion, fraud and misrepresentation.

quiz.q: Which section defines coercion, and what does it require?
options: Section 15 — an act forbidden by the Penal Code, or unlawful detention of property
Section 17 — a false suggestion of fact
quiz.why: The statutory definition is much narrower than 'pressure', which is where English duress reasoning goes wrong here.

quiz.q: When is mere silence fraud under s 17?
options: Where there is a duty to speak, or silence is equivalent to speech
Always, if a material fact is withheld
quiz.why: The explanation to s 17 states both limbs. Silence alone is not fraud.

quiz.q: What distinguishes s 18 misrepresentation from s 17 fraud?
options: The maker believes the assertion to be true
The statement is about the future
quiz.why: Section 18 covers a positive assertion not warranted by the information of the person making it, though believed true.

quiz.q: A party has received an advantage under an agreement discovered to be void. Which provision requires restoration?
quiz.why: Section 66 does the work restitution does elsewhere.

quiz.q: What is the age of majority for the purposes of capacity to contract?
quiz.why: Age of Majority Act 1971, read with s 11 of the Contracts Act 1950.

lessons.title: Breach, damages, and the trouble with an agreed sum
lessons.summary: Section 74 measures compensation, section 75 governs a sum named in the contract, and the law on the second has moved in Malaysia within the last decade.

sections.h: What counts as breach, and what the innocent party may do

body.text: When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified by words or conduct his acquiescence in its continuance.
Termination is an election, and it can be lost. A party who continues to press for performance after a repudiation may be held to have affirmed, and affirmation leaves him with damages only.

Time is dealt with by ss 56 and 57. Whether time is of the essence is a question of the parties' intention, and a stipulation as to time in a contract for the sale of goods or land is not automatically essential.

When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by the breach is entitled to receive compensation for any loss or damage caused to him which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage.

The two limbs will look familiar: this is the rule in *Hadley v Baxendale*, enacted. That matters for how you argue it — the starting point is the statutory words, with the English cases as illustration of how the limbs have been applied, not as the source of the rule.

The explanation to s 74 adds that in estimating loss, the means available for remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance must be taken into account. That is the statutory foothold for mitigation.

sections.h: Section 75, and the change of direction

body.text: When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, the party complaining of the breach is entitled to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named.

For a long period the Malaysian position, from *Selva Kumar a/l Murugiah v Thiagarajah a/l Retnasamy*, was that a plaintiff relying on s 75 had to prove actual loss, and could recover only what was proved, subject to the named sum as a ceiling. The named sum was, in effect, a cap and nothing more.

That was revisited in *Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd (in liquidation) v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd*, where the Federal Court reformulated the approach, drawing on the reasoning in *Cavendish Square Holding BV v Makdessi* and directing attention to whether the clause protects a legitimate interest and whether the sum is out of all proportion to that interest.

This is the single most important 'check before you rely on it' point in the contract module. State the sequence, name both cases, and check whether anything has been decided since — an answer that gives only *Selva Kumar* is out of date, and one that gives only *Cubic Electronics* has not shown it understands what changed.

Damages are the primary remedy; specific performance is discretionary and governed by the Specific Relief Act 1950. Section 11 sets out the cases in which it may be granted, and s 20 the cases in which it cannot — including where compensation in money is an adequate relief, and where the contract requires continuous supervision.

Land is the ordinary example of a subject-matter for which damages are treated as inadequate, which is why specific performance is a live remedy in a sale of land and rarely in a sale of ordinary goods.

The Specific Relief Act is a separate statute with its own scheme. Do not answer a specific performance question out of the Contracts Act, and do not import English equitable discretion in place of the Act's sections.

Establish the contract, then the breach, then whether the innocent party terminated or affirmed, then the measure. Only then reach any agreed sum. Answers that start with the liquidated damages clause tend to skip the question whether there is a recoverable loss at all.

quiz.q: Section 74 of the Contracts Act 1950 enacts which familiar rule?
options: The rule in Hadley v Baxendale
The rule in Hong Kong Fir
quiz.why: The two limbs — loss arising naturally, and loss within the parties' contemplation — are the statutory form of it.

quiz.q: Which case reformulated the Malaysian approach to a sum named in the contract under s 75?
options: Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San
quiz.why: The Federal Court there moved away from the strict proof-of-actual-loss requirement, drawing on Cavendish v Makdessi.

quiz.q: Under s 40, what may a promisee do when the other party refuses to perform in its entirety?
options: Put an end to the contract, unless he has acquiesced in its continuance
Nothing until the time for performance passes
quiz.why: Termination is an election and it can be lost by affirmation.

quiz.q: Which statute governs specific performance in Malaysia?
quiz.why: It has its own scheme, in ss 11 and 20 among others; do not answer out of the Contracts Act.

quiz.q: Why is specific performance a live remedy in a sale of land?
options: Damages are treated as inadequate for land
Land contracts are always in writing
The National Land Code requires it
quiz.why: Adequacy of damages is the gateway question under the Specific Relief Act.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of analysis in a remedies question?
options: Contract, breach, termination or affirmation, measure, then any agreed sum
quiz.why: Starting at the clause skips the question whether there is a recoverable loss at all.

reading.where: the chapters on discharge and remedies
for the fuller treatment of s 75 and the Selva Kumar line

lessons.source: Contracts Act 1950 ss 40, 56, 57, 74, 75; Specific Relief Act 1950 ss 11 and 20; Selva Kumar a/l Murugiah v Thiagarajah a/l Retnasamy [1995] 1 MLJ 817 (FC); Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd [2019] 2 MLJ 806 (FC).
lessons.verify: Both citations must be checked in a report you can hold, and you must check whether any Federal Court decision after Cubic Electronics has qualified it. The s 75 position has changed once and could change again; this is the paragraph in the whole module most likely to go stale.

lessons.title: Causation, remoteness, and the plaintiff's own fault
lessons.summary: Duty and breach get you halfway. The other half — factual causation, legal causation, remoteness, and apportionment under s 12 of the Civil Law Act 1956 — is where negligence claims are actually won and lost.

sections.h: Factual causation: the but-for test and its limits

body.text: The plaintiff must show that, but for the defendant's breach, the damage would not have occurred.
body.source: Standard common law test of factual causation; applied in Malaysia

body.text: A casualty officer sends away a man who has been poisoned. He dies. If he would have died even with treatment, the negligence caused no loss, and the claim fails on causation however plain the breach.

The test breaks down in two familiar situations: multiple sufficient causes, where each alone would have caused the damage, and cases of scientific uncertainty about which of several exposures caused the injury. Both have generated exceptional approaches, and both should be identified as exceptions rather than used as the general rule.

A later act may break the chain. A deliberate wrongful act by a third party usually does; a foreseeable act, or one the defendant's own negligence made likely, usually does not. The plaintiff's own unreasonable conduct can also break it.
Do not use novus actus and contributory negligence interchangeably. The first defeats the claim; the second reduces it. Choosing the wrong one is a substantive error dressed as a vocabulary slip.

sections.h: Remoteness: the kind of damage, not its extent

body.text: A defendant is liable only for damage of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable. Where the kind of damage is foreseeable, it is no answer that its extent was not.
body.source: The Wagon Mound (No 1); applied in the Malaysian courts

body.text: The 'eggshell skull' principle sits inside this: a defendant takes the victim as found. Foreseeability governs the type of injury; the plaintiff's particular susceptibility governs how bad it turns out to be, and does not reduce the claim.

Where any person suffers damage as the result partly of his own fault and partly of the fault of any other person, a claim shall not be defeated by reason of the fault of the person suffering the damage, but the damages recoverable shall be reduced to such extent as the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in the responsibility for the damage.

Before that section, contributory negligence was a complete defence. It is now an apportionment exercise, and the answer to a problem should give a reasoned proportion rather than a bare assertion that damages 'will be reduced'.

Two related statutory points belong in the same answer where the facts raise them: the Civil Law Act also governs claims arising out of death — the dependency claim and the estate claim — and the heads of damage recoverable are constrained by the Act rather than at large.

Damages for death and personal injury in Malaysia are shaped by statute in ways that differ from English practice. Check the current text of the Civil Law Act 1956 before stating what is recoverable and how it is calculated.

Take the elements in order and do not skip forward. Duty, breach, factual causation, legal causation, remoteness, damage, then defences and apportionment. The order is not stylistic: each step assumes the one before, and an answer that argues remoteness before establishing breach is arguing about nothing.

quiz.q: A doctor negligently sends away a patient who would have died anyway. What defeats the claim?
quiz.why: The breach caused no loss, so the claim fails at causation however clear the breach.

quiz.q: What is the effect of contributory negligence in Malaysia?
options: Damages are apportioned under s 12 of the Civil Law Act 1956
It breaks the chain of causation
quiz.why: Section 12 replaced the complete defence with apportionment.

quiz.q: Which is the correct statement of the remoteness rule?
options: The kind of damage must be foreseeable; the extent need not be
Both kind and extent must be foreseeable
Neither need be foreseeable if breach is proved
Only economic loss must be foreseeable
quiz.why: The Wagon Mound test, with the eggshell skull principle sitting inside it.

quiz.q: What is the difference between novus actus interveniens and contributory negligence?
options: The first defeats the claim; the second reduces it
The first applies only to third parties, the second only to defendants
The first is statutory, the second is common law
quiz.why: Using them interchangeably is a substantive error, not a vocabulary slip.

quiz.q: In what order should a negligence answer proceed?
options: Duty, breach, causation, remoteness, damage, defences
quiz.why: Each step assumes the one before it; arguing remoteness before breach is arguing about nothing.

reading.where: the chapters on causation, remoteness and defences

lessons.source: Civil Law Act 1956 s 12; The Wagon Mound (No 1) [1961] AC 388 as applied in Malaysia; standard common law on factual and legal causation.
lessons.verify: Check s 12 and the death-and-personal-injury provisions of the Civil Law Act 1956 against the current text, and check the current Malaysian authority on the duty of care test before assuming any particular English formulation applies here.

lessons.title: Defamation: the three elements, and the defences that matter
lessons.summary: Defamatory meaning, reference to the plaintiff, and publication. The Defamation Act 1957 then governs the defences, and the distinction between libel and slander still does work here.

items: **The words are defamatory** — they tend to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally, or expose him to hatred, ridicule or contempt, or cause him to be shunned or avoided.
**They refer to the plaintiff** — expressly, or in a way that reasonable readers with knowledge of the surrounding circumstances would understand as referring to him. Naming is not necessary.
**They were published** — communicated to at least one person other than the plaintiff.

body.text: All three must be established before any defence is reached. An answer that opens with qualified privilege has assumed the case it should be proving.

Libel is in permanent form; slander in transient form. The distinction matters because slander is generally actionable only on proof of special damage, with exceptions. The Defamation Act 1957 preserves and modifies the categories.

Words spoken and published which impute unchastity or adultery to any woman or girl, and words calculated to disparage a person in any office, profession, calling, trade or business held or carried on by him at the time of publication, do not require proof of special damage.

Publication online has made the permanent-or-transient line harder to apply than it sounds. Check the current Malaysian authority on how internet publication is classified before assuming it is libel.

items: **Justification** — the imputation is true in substance and in fact. Section 8 of the Act provides that a defence of justification does not fail merely because the truth of every charge is not proved, if the remaining charges do not materially injure the plaintiff's reputation given the truth of the rest.
**Fair comment** — an honest comment, on a matter of public interest, based on facts truly stated. Section 9 addresses the position where not every allegation of fact is proved true.
**Absolute privilege** — statements in Parliament and in judicial proceedings, which no malice defeats.
**Qualified privilege** — an occasion where the maker has a duty or interest in making the statement and the recipient a corresponding interest in receiving it. Defeated by malice.
**Apology and payment into court**, under the Act's own provisions, which have procedural conditions attached.
**Offer of amends**, again on the statute's terms.

body.text: Whether, and how far, the *Reynolds* line of responsible-journalism privilege forms part of Malaysian law has been argued in the Malaysian courts and should not be assumed either way. If your answer needs it, cite a Malaysian decision.

Malice is not an element of the tort. It matters in two places: it defeats qualified privilege, and it defeats fair comment. Establishing that a publisher was hostile does not by itself establish liability, and saying so is a cheap way to show you know where malice sits.
Damages are at large and take account of the gravity of the imputation, the extent of publication, and the defendant's conduct including any apology or its absence.

quiz.q: Which three elements must a defamation plaintiff prove?
options: Defamatory meaning, reference to the plaintiff, publication
quiz.why: Only after all three are established does any defence arise.

quiz.q: What does 'publication' mean in defamation?
options: Communication to at least one person other than the plaintiff
Circulation to the public at large
quiz.why: One third party is enough; it does not require mass circulation.

quiz.q: Where does malice bite in a defamation action?
options: It defeats qualified privilege and fair comment
It is an element of the tort
quiz.why: Malice is not part of the cause of action. It answers two of the defences.

quiz.q: What is the effect of s 8 of the Defamation Act 1957?
options: Justification does not fail merely because every charge is not proved true
Fair comment requires no factual basis
Absolute privilege extends to the press
quiz.why: It saves a justification defence where the unproved charges do not materially injure reputation given the rest.

quiz.q: Why does the libel-slander distinction still matter?
options: Slander generally requires proof of special damage
Slander has a longer limitation period
quiz.why: Subject to the statutory exceptions, including the professional-disparagement category.

lessons.source: Defamation Act 1957, in particular ss 4, 5, 8 and 9; standard common law elements of the tort.
lessons.verify: Check the current text of the Defamation Act 1957 — section numbering and content should be confirmed — and find current Malaysian authority on the classification of internet publication and on whether Reynolds privilege has been received here.

lessons.title: Dealings, charges and caveats: how an interest is protected
lessons.summary: Under the Code an interest exists when it is registered. Everything else — contracts, caveats, liens — is machinery for getting there or for stopping someone else getting there first.

sections.h: Registration creates; a contract does not

body.text: Any dealing under the National Land Code is effective to pass or create an interest in land only upon registration; until then the instrument passes nothing at law.
body.source: National Land Code, Division IV on dealings, read with the registration provisions

body.text: A sale and purchase agreement therefore gives the purchaser a contractual right and, in equity, an interest capable of protection — but not title. Between exchange and registration the purchaser is exposed, and the whole of the caveat machinery exists because of that gap.
Do not write that a purchaser 'owns' the land on completion of the agreement. The register decides ownership, and this is the mistake that unravels an entire answer on priorities.

sections.h: Charges, and what a chargee may do

body.text: A charge is the Code's security interest over registered land. It is created by a registered instrument and gives the chargee no possession — the security is the ability to enforce, not to occupy.

items: On default, the chargee serves the statutory notice of default and, if it is not remedied, may apply for an order for sale.
For land held under **Registry title**, application is to the **High Court** for an order for sale.
For land held under **Land Office title**, application is to the **Land Administrator**.
The court will order sale unless the chargor shows **cause to the contrary**, which is a narrow concept and not a general discretion.

body.text: The Registry-title and Land-Office-title routes are different tracks with different provisions and different appeal routes. Identify which title the land is held under before you say where the application goes; getting this wrong is the standard way to lose the method marks in a charge question.
A private caveat may be entered by a person claiming title to the land, or claiming any registrable interest in it, or claiming to be beneficially entitled under any trust affecting it.

A caveat does not create an interest. It prevents the registration of dealings while it is in force, which buys time for the claim to be determined. It lapses after the statutory period unless extended, and it may be removed on application by a person aggrieved.

On such an application the caveator must show that the claim discloses a serious question to be tried, and that the balance of convenience favours maintaining the caveat until trial. That is the same shape as the test for an interlocutory injunction, and for the same reason.
A caveat entered without reasonable cause exposes the caveator to compensation. It is not a costless holding move, and advising a client to lodge one 'just in case' is advice with a price attached.

items: **Registrar's caveat** — entered by the Registrar to protect the interests of the Federation or a State, or a person under disability, or to prevent fraud or improper dealing.

**Lien-holder's caveat** — the mechanism by which a deposit of the issue document of title, coupled with the intention to create security, is protected. The lien becomes enforceable once the caveat is entered.
**Trust caveat** — protecting land held on trust.

body.text: A question that mentions a deposited title document is almost always a lien-holder's caveat question, and identifying it by that cue is faster than reasoning from first principles.

Section 340 gives the registered proprietor an indefeasible title, subject to the exceptions in s 340(2). *Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San* restored deferred indefeasibility: a person who acquires title through a void or forged instrument does not obtain an indefeasible title, though a subsequent purchaser in good faith and for value may.

*Adorna Properties Sdn Bhd v Boonsom Boonyanit* held the opposite and stood for nine years. If a source you are reading relies on it without noting that it was departed from, stop trusting that source.

quiz.q: When does a dealing pass an interest in registered land?
options: On delivery of the title document
quiz.why: The register creates the interest. Everything before registration is contractual or equitable only.

quiz.q: What does a private caveat do?
options: Prevents registration of dealings while it is in force
Creates an interest in the land
quiz.why: It is a freeze, not an interest. It buys time for the underlying claim to be determined.

quiz.q: On an application to remove a private caveat, what must the caveator show?
options: A serious question to be tried and that the balance of convenience favours the caveat
That he will succeed at trial
quiz.why: The same shape as an interlocutory injunction test, for the same reason.

quiz.q: A chargee seeks an order for sale of land held under Registry title. Where does the application go?
quiz.why: Registry title goes to the High Court; Land Office title goes to the Land Administrator.

quiz.q: Which case restored deferred indefeasibility under s 340?
options: Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San
quiz.why: Tan Ying Hong departed from Adorna Properties, which had held for immediate indefeasibility.

quiz.q: Facts mention a deposited issue document of title as security. Which caveat is in issue?
quiz.why: Deposit of the title document plus intention to secure is the lien-holder's caveat cue.

reading.where: the chapters on dealings, charges and caveats

lessons.source: National Land Code, Division IV (dealings), the charge and order-for-sale provisions, ss 320-330 on caveats and s 340 on indefeasibility; Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC); Adorna Properties Sdn Bhd v Boonsom Boonyanit [2001] 1 MLJ 241 (FC).
lessons.verify: The Code was revised in 2020 and section numbering must be checked against the current text before any section is cited. Check the caveat lapse period and the order-for-sale provisions in particular, and confirm both case citations in a report you can hold.

lessons.title: Directors' duties, and what a member can do about a breach
lessons.summary: The Companies Act 2016 states the duties in statute. The remedies — oppression, the statutory derivative action, and winding up on the just and equitable ground — belong to different people and answer different complaints.

sections.h: The duties, as the Act states them

body.text: A director shall at all times exercise his powers in accordance with this Act, for a proper purpose and in good faith in the best interest of the company.

A director shall exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence with the knowledge, skill and experience which may reasonably be expected of a director having the same responsibilities, and any additional knowledge, skill and experience which the director in fact has.

The first is a fiduciary duty in statutory form; the second is the duty of care, with an objective floor and a subjective addition. Section 218 deals separately with the improper use of the company's property, position, or information.

Section 214 introduces the business judgement rule: a director who makes a business judgement in good faith for a proper purpose, without a material personal interest, on a reasonably informed basis and in the reasonable belief that it is in the best interest of the company, is taken to have met the requirement of s 213(2).

The starting point is that a wrong done to the company is the company's to complain of, and the company acts through its board or its members in general meeting. That is why an individual member who is unhappy about a breach of duty cannot simply sue.

The most common error is to reach for a derivative action or an oppression petition without first asking who suffered the loss. A diminution in the value of every member's shares because the company was harmed is reflective loss, and it is the company's claim, not the member's.

sections.h: The three routes, and which complaint each answers

items: **Oppression (s 346).** A member may complain that the affairs of the company are being conducted, or the powers of the directors exercised, in a manner oppressive to one or more members, or in disregard of their interests. The complaint is about how the member has been treated. The court's powers on such a petition are wide.

**Statutory derivative action (ss 347-350).** A member, a director, or the Registrar may with the **leave of the court** bring proceedings **on behalf of the company** to enforce the company's own right. The complaint is the company's; the applicant must show good faith and that the action is prima facie in the company's best interest.

**Winding up on the just and equitable ground.** The court may wind the company up where it is just and equitable to do so — most often in a quasi-partnership where the relationship of trust has broken down. It is the remedy of last resort and it kills the company.

body.text: Choosing between them is the whole of the analysis in most problem questions. An oppression petition and a derivative action are not alternatives to be pleaded together without thought; they proceed on inconsistent premises about whose right is being vindicated.

sections.h: Separate legal personality, and its limits

body.text: A company incorporated under the Act is a body corporate with its own legal personality, capable of suing and being sued in its own name. That is the foundation of everything above, and of *Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd*.

The corporate veil is lifted rarely and on stated grounds — fraud, or the use of the corporate form as a device to evade an existing obligation, or where a statute so provides. Section 540 of the Act deals with fraudulent trading and imposes personal liability on those knowingly party to it.

'Lifting the veil in the interests of justice' is not a ground, however often it is asserted. Check the current Malaysian authority before advancing it, and prefer a statutory route where one is available.

The Act removed the mandatory annual general meeting for private companies and provides for written resolutions instead; public companies must still hold an AGM. Notice periods, quorum and the distinction between ordinary and special resolutions are governed by the Act and the constitution, and a procedural irregularity may be cured or may invalidate the resolution depending on the provision engaged.

This is an area where the 2016 Act changed the law substantially from the Companies Act 1965. Any source written before 2017 should be treated as describing a repealed statute until you have checked it.

quiz.q: Which provision states the duty to act in good faith in the best interest of the company?
quiz.why: Section 213(1) is the fiduciary duty in statutory form; 213(2) is the duty of care.

quiz.q: A member is unhappy that directors have harmed the company, reducing the value of all shares. What is the difficulty with a personal claim?
options: The loss is reflective; the claim belongs to the company
quiz.why: A wrong to the company is the company's to complain of — hence the derivative action machinery.

quiz.q: What does a statutory derivative action require?
options: Leave of the court, good faith, and that it is prima facie in the company's best interest
quiz.why: Sections 347-350 set out the leave requirement and the criteria.

quiz.q: Which remedy answers a complaint about how a member has been treated?
quiz.why: Section 346 is about the conduct of the company's affairs in a manner oppressive to a member.

quiz.q: What does the business judgement rule in s 214 do?
options: Deems the duty of care met where its conditions are satisfied
Removes the duty of care for private companies
quiz.why: It is a safe harbour for s 213(2), not for the fiduciary duty in s 213(1).

quiz.q: Why should a source published in 2015 be treated with care in this module?
options: The Companies Act 2016 substantially changed the law
Company law is a State matter
quiz.why: The 1965 Act was repealed; a pre-2017 text is describing a repealed statute until checked.

lessons.source: Companies Act 2016 ss 213, 214, 218, 346, 347-350, 540; Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22.
lessons.verify: Check every section number against the current text of Act 777, and check the current Malaysian authority on lifting the corporate veil and on the leave criteria for a statutory derivative action before relying on the summary above.

lessons.title: Burden and standard of proof under the Evidence Act
lessons.summary: Sections 101 to 106 distribute the burden. They distinguish the burden of proof from the burden of adducing evidence, and a great deal turns on which one a provision is talking about.

sections.h: The two burdens the Act distinguishes

body.text: Whoever desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability, dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist. When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person.
The burden of proof in a suit or proceeding lies on that person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side.

Section 101 states the legal burden — the risk of non-persuasion, which does not shift. Section 102 identifies who carries it by asking who loses on a blank record. Section 103 then places the burden of proving any particular fact on the person who wishes the court to believe it, which is the evidential burden and which does shift as the case proceeds.

Answers routinely say 'the burden shifted to the defendant' when they mean the evidential burden. Say which one you mean. The legal burden in a criminal case shifts only where a statute makes it shift.

Section 105, met in the criminal law module, places on the accused the burden of proving circumstances that bring the case within a general exception in the Penal Code or within any special exception or proviso in the law defining the offence, and directs the court to presume the absence of such circumstances.
That is a genuine legal burden on the accused, discharged on the balance of probabilities. It is the principal statutory exception to the rule that the prosecution proves everything.

sections.h: Section 106 and facts especially within knowledge

body.text: When any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon him.

Section 106 is the most over-used provision in the Act. It does not relieve the prosecution of proving its case; it applies to a specific fact peculiarly within a person's knowledge — a licence, an authority, a reason for being somewhere — and it cannot be used to reverse the general burden. An answer that deploys s 106 to shift the whole case has misread it.

A presumption tells the court what it may or must infer. The Act distinguishes 'may presume' — a discretion — from 'shall presume' — mandatory unless disproved — from 'conclusive proof', which admits no evidence in rebuttal. Section 4 defines the three.

Section 114 lists facts the court may presume, and illustration (g) is the one that appears constantly: that evidence which could be and is not produced would, if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it.

Illustration (g) is permissive and is not drawn automatically from every gap in the evidence. The party inviting the inference must show that the evidence was available and material, and that no explanation for its absence has been given.

None of this arises until the evidence is admissible. Section 5 admits evidence of facts in issue and of relevant facts, and relevance is defined by the Act, not at large. A fact is not admissible because it is interesting, probative-sounding, or fair to admit; it is admissible because a section makes it relevant.
Keep the two questions apart in writing: first, is this admissible under a named section; second, who has to prove what, and to what standard. Merging them is the fastest way to a confused answer.

quiz.q: Which section states that the burden lies on the person who would fail if no evidence were given?
quiz.why: Section 102 identifies who carries the legal burden by asking who loses on a blank record.

quiz.q: What is the effect of s 105 on an accused relying on a general exception?
options: He carries a legal burden, on the balance of probabilities
He carries an evidential burden only
The prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt
The exception is presumed in his favour
quiz.why: The court presumes the absence of the circumstances and the accused must prove them.

quiz.q: What is the correct scope of s 106?
options: A specific fact especially within a person's knowledge
The whole of the defence case
Any fact the prosecution cannot easily prove
quiz.why: It cannot be used to reverse the general burden, and this is the commonest misuse of the Act.

quiz.q: What does 'shall presume' mean under s 4?
options: The court must presume the fact unless it is disproved
The court may presume the fact
No evidence in rebuttal is allowed
quiz.why: 'May presume' is a discretion; 'conclusive proof' admits no rebuttal.

quiz.q: When may an adverse inference be drawn under illustration (g) to s 114?
options: Where material evidence was available, withheld, and unexplained
From any gap in the evidence
Whenever a witness is not called
quiz.why: It is permissive and conditional, not a default.

quiz.q: What must be established before any question of burden arises?
options: That the evidence is admissible under a named section
quiz.why: Relevancy is the gate, and it is defined by the Act rather than at large.

reading.where: the chapters on burden of proof and presumptions

lessons.verify: Check the sections against the current text of Act 56, and check current authority on the conditions for drawing an adverse inference under s 114(g) — it is frequently argued and the formulations differ.

lessons.title: Getting to the end early: summary disposal and interim relief
lessons.summary: Most civil cases never reach trial. Order 14, Order 18 rule 19 and Order 29 of the Rules of Court 2012 are how they end, and each has a different threshold.

body.text: A plaintiff who says the defence is hopeless may apply for judgment without trial. The application is supported by affidavit verifying the facts and stating a belief that there is no defence.

The defendant resists by showing an issue or question in dispute which ought to be tried, or that there ought for some other reason to be a trial. Where he does, unconditional leave to defend follows; where the defence is shadowy, leave may be conditional.
The threshold is not whether the defence will succeed. It is whether there is a triable issue, and an answer that weighs the merits as if at trial has applied the wrong test.

items: The court may strike out a pleading which discloses no reasonable cause of action or defence; or is scandalous, frivolous or vexatious; or may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial; or is otherwise an abuse of process.
On the first ground, no evidence is admissible: the question is taken on the pleading as it stands.
The jurisdiction is used sparingly and only in plain and obvious cases. A difficult point of law is not, by itself, a reason to strike out.

body.text: The distinction from Order 14 is worth stating: Order 14 says the defence has no substance on the evidence; Order 18 rule 19 says the pleading is bad as a document.

The applicant must show a serious question to be tried; that damages would not be an adequate remedy; and that the balance of convenience lies in favour of granting the injunction. An undertaking in damages is ordinarily required.
body.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 29; the American Cyanamid approach as applied in Malaysia

body.text: The Malaysian courts have their own gloss on this, and there is authority requiring the applicant to establish a *bona fide* serious question rather than merely a question that is not frivolous. Where an application is made *ex parte*, the duty of full and frank disclosure is strict and a breach of it is itself a ground for discharge.
A mandatory interlocutory injunction — one requiring something to be done rather than restrained — attracts a higher threshold. Identify which kind you are asking for before you state the test.

sections.h: Limitation, which decides more cases than any of these

body.text: The Limitation Act 1953 sets six years for actions founded on contract or on tort, running from the date on which the cause of action accrued. Different periods apply to actions to recover land and to certain other claims, and there are provisions on disability, acknowledgment and part payment.

Limitation is a defence that must be pleaded; a court will not take the point for a defendant who has not. Check the current text of the Act for the period applicable to the particular claim before advising — and check whether any special limitation provision in another statute displaces it.

A judgment is not money. Enforcement is a separate exercise — writ of seizure and sale, garnishee proceedings, judgment debtor summons, charging order, or winding-up or bankruptcy proceedings where the debtor cannot pay. An advice that stops at 'the plaintiff will obtain judgment' has stopped one step early.

quiz.q: What must a defendant show to resist summary judgment under Order 14?
options: A triable issue, or some other reason for a trial
That the plaintiff acted in bad faith
quiz.why: The threshold is a triable issue, not the merits as they would be resolved at trial.

quiz.q: On an application to strike out for disclosing no reasonable cause of action, what evidence is admissible?
options: None — the pleading is taken as it stands
quiz.why: Under that limb of O 18 r 19 the question is decided on the pleading alone.

quiz.q: Which is not part of the interlocutory injunction test?
options: Whether the applicant will probably win at trial
A serious question to be tried
quiz.why: The court does not try the merits at the interlocutory stage.

quiz.q: What is the special obligation on an ex parte application?
options: Leave of a judge in chambers
quiz.why: Breach of the duty is itself a ground for discharging the order.

quiz.q: What is the general limitation period for an action founded on contract or tort?
quiz.why: Limitation Act 1953, subject to the special periods and to any displacing statute.

quiz.q: Why is 'the plaintiff will obtain judgment' an incomplete advice?
quiz.why: A judgment is a right to be paid, not payment; the enforcement route has to be advised on too.

for the rules themselves with commentary

lessons.source: Rules of Court 2012, Orders 14, 18 r 19 and 29; Limitation Act 1953 s 6; American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd [1975] AC 396 as applied in Malaysia.
lessons.verify: Check the Rules of Court 2012 for amendments, and check current Malaysian authority on the interlocutory injunction test — the local gloss on American Cyanamid is stated differently in different judgments and should be cited from a Malaysian decision, not an English one.

lessons.title: Natural justice, legitimate expectation, and the limits of review
lessons.summary: Procedural impropriety is the ground most often made out and most often pleaded badly. The two rules are old, narrow and precise, and legitimate expectation extends them only so far.

sections.h: Two rules, not a general fairness power

items: **Audi alteram partem** — a person liable to be affected by a decision must be given notice of the case against him and a fair opportunity to answer it. What that requires varies with the decision: an oral hearing is not always necessary, reasons are not always required, and legal representation is not always allowed.

**Nemo judex in causa sua** — no one may be a judge in his own cause. Actual bias is rare; the working test is whether a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real danger, or real possibility, of bias.

body.text: Check which formulation of the bias test the Malaysian courts currently apply, and cite a Malaysian decision for it. 'Real danger' and 'real possibility' have both been used, and the difference is examinable.

sections.h: What the content of the duty depends on

body.text: The intensity of the procedural requirement varies with what is at stake, the statutory framework, and the character of the decision-maker. A decision affecting livelihood or liberty attracts more; a preliminary or investigatory step attracts less. Say what the facts require and why, rather than asserting that 'natural justice applies'.

A licence is revoked without warning and without the holder being told what he is said to have done. That is a straightforward *audi alteram partem* case. A licence is refused on renewal after a hearing at which the applicant made representations but was refused legal representation — that is arguable, and the argument is about content, not existence.

A legitimate expectation arises from a clear and unambiguous representation, or from a settled practice, that a person will be treated in a particular way. It is most secure as a **procedural** expectation — that he will be consulted, or heard, before a change.

A **substantive** legitimate expectation — that the benefit itself will be conferred — is more contested. Its reception in Malaysia should be checked against current authority before it is asserted, and an answer that treats it as settled is overstating the position.

An expectation cannot be legitimate if the representation was outside the decision-maker's power. A public body cannot bind itself to act unlawfully, and an answer that overlooks that has usually reached the wrong conclusion.

sections.h: The other grounds, and how far review goes

items: **Illegality** — the decision-maker misdirected itself in law, acted outside its powers, took into account irrelevant considerations or failed to take into account relevant ones, or acted for an improper purpose.
**Irrationality** — a decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have come to it.
**Procedural impropriety** — the two rules above, and failure to observe a mandatory procedural requirement in the empowering statute.
**Proportionality** — argued increasingly, and accepted in Malaysia in the constitutional context; its status as a free-standing head of administrative review should be checked rather than assumed.

body.text: Review is of the decision-making process, not the merits. The Malaysian courts have gone further than the English in places — there is authority allowing a court to substitute its own decision in an appropriate case rather than remitting — and that line of authority should be cited if you rely on it.

items: Application for judicial review is made under Order 53 of the Rules of Court 2012, and requires **leave**.
There is a time limit — the application for leave must be made promptly and within the period prescribed by the rule, running from the date when the grounds arose.
The applicant must be **adversely affected** by the decision. The Malaysian test for standing has been stated in the Federal Court and is narrower than the English 'sufficient interest'.
Relief includes certiorari, prohibition, mandamus, declaration and injunction, and damages may be claimed in the same proceedings in the circumstances the rule allows.

body.text: Getting the procedure wrong ends the case regardless of its merits. Check the current Order 53 text for the time limit and the leave requirement before advising on any application.

quiz.q: What does audi alteram partem require?
options: Notice of the case and a fair opportunity to answer it
An oral hearing in every case
quiz.why: The content varies with the decision; the core is notice and an opportunity to answer.

quiz.q: Which is the practical test for bias?
options: Whether a fair-minded and informed observer would see a real danger or possibility of bias
Whether the decision-maker was actually biased
quiz.why: Actual bias is rarely provable; the objective test does the work. Check which formulation the Malaysian courts currently use.

quiz.q: Which form of legitimate expectation is most secure?
options: Procedural — that the person will be heard before a change
Substantive — that the benefit will be conferred
quiz.why: The substantive form is more contested and its reception in Malaysia should be checked, not assumed.

quiz.q: A public body represents that it will act in a way the statute does not permit. Can a legitimate expectation arise?
options: No — a body cannot bind itself to act unlawfully
Yes, if the representation was clear
Yes, if the applicant relied on it
Only if the representation was in writing
quiz.why: An expectation outside the decision-maker's power cannot be legitimate.

quiz.q: What must an applicant for judicial review under Order 53 obtain first?
quiz.why: Leave is a threshold requirement, and the application must also be made within the prescribed time.

quiz.q: What is the Malaysian standing requirement for judicial review?
options: That the applicant is adversely affected by the decision
Any member of the public may apply
Only a party to the original proceedings
quiz.why: The 'adversely affected' test has been stated in the Federal Court and is narrower than the English formulation.

reading.where: the chapters on natural justice and legitimate expectation, read as comparative material rather than as Malaysian law

lessons.source: Rules of Court 2012, Order 53; the common law grounds of review as received in Malaysia; the Malaysian authorities on standing, on remedy, and on legitimate expectation.
lessons.verify: Every proposition here needs a Malaysian citation before use: the bias formulation, the standing test, the status of substantive legitimate expectation, whether proportionality is a free-standing head of review, and the current Order 53 time limit. Wade and Forsyth is English and states English law.
